paper.title: Experimental Evidence on the Learning Impact of Generative AI
paper.version_read: September 2026, as dated on the title page (PDF p. 1); the manuscript required by extraction-spec Rule 6.
paper.one_line_finding: AI access showed no detectable change in between-student essay similarity during access (coefficient 0.001, SE 0.007; control mean 0.774) or one week later without AI (-0.005, SE 0.013; control mean 0.762; p. 39, Table 5 Panel C).

studies.label: Two-session laboratory experiment: analytical essays with randomized AI access, then unaided writing approximately one week later
studies.cluster_se_treatment: Students were individually randomized to computers within their chosen time slot, then the two parallel labs were randomly assigned opposite AI conditions (PDF p. 6, Section 2.1; PDF p. 54, Figure A3 notes). The printed eight time slots describe randomization strata; no per-arm cluster count is separately printed. clusters_per_arm is null rather than a derived count of lab-by-time-slot delivery groups. The paper reports student-level heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors with time-slot fixed effects (PDF pp. 11-12, Section 3.3). No lab/time-slot clustering or adjustment for dependence between similarity scores sharing essays is reported.

arms.name: AI-allowed
arms.description: Any generative AI tool permitted during Session One learning and essay writing; a dedicated ChatGPT (GPT-4o) account was supplied. Standard online resources were also permitted. AI and other external resources were prohibited for all knowledge tests and for the Session Two essay (PDF pp. 7-10, Sections 2.1-2.2; PDF p. 53, Figure A2). Arm counts refer to assigned sign-ups and the Session One study sample, not the outcome-specific essay sample.

arms.name: AI-forbidden
arms.description: Generative AI prohibited during Session One learning and essay writing; standard online resources such as Google, Wikipedia, and the college library website were permitted. AI and other external resources were prohibited for all knowledge tests and for the Session Two essay (PDF pp. 7-10, Sections 2.1-2.2; PDF p. 53, Figure A2). Arm counts refer to assigned sign-ups and the Session One study sample, not the outcome-specific essay sample.

studies.task: Middlebury College undergraduates read about randomly assigned blockchain technology, carbon capture, or CRISPR gene editing and write an analytical essay, then write to a complementary prompt on the same topic without AI or other resources in the later session (PDF pp. 7-10, Sections 2.1-3.1).

ai_tool.name: ChatGPT (GPT-4o); any generative AI tool was permitted
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 8, Section 2.1, Treatment; the model release year is not printed

preregistration.where: AEA RCT Registry, AEARCTR-0015806, named and linked on PDF p. 1; the pre-analysis plan is discussed on PDF p. 13, Section 3.4. The external registration and plan were not independently retrieved.
preregistration.primary_outcome: The paper explicitly identifies overall essay quality and the average quality index as the pre-analysis plan primary essay-based outcomes (PDF p. 13, Section 3.4). Within-group similarity is an ancillary essay-writing characteristic.

estimates.outcome: Within-group similarity, Session One essays (AI available)
estimates.question: across_people
estimates.measure_detail: For each student, average pairwise cosine similarity between that student's essay embedding and all other essays in the same assigned treatment × topic × prompt cell. A sentence-embedding model fine-tuned from MPNet is named; its exact checkpoint is not stated. The analysis uses a student-level score, with an essay produced in each session; higher similarity means less diversity across writers (PDF p. 14, Section 3.4; PDF p. 41, Table 5 notes).

regression.model: Intent-to-treat OLS coefficient on assignment to AI-allowed, with Session One time-slot fixed effects and double-lasso-selected controls. The outcome is the student-level average within-group cosine similarity in raw units (PDF pp. 11-12, Section 3.3; PDF p. 41, Table 5 notes).

paper_effect.standardizer: None. This is the additional treatment-on-the-treated coefficient in raw cosine-similarity units, estimated by two-stage least squares instrumenting actual ChatGPT use with randomized AI-access assignment. It is not a standardized effect.

estimates.notes: The randomized-access ITT coefficient and its robust standard error are in regression. The additional printed instrumental-variable TOT coefficient and its robust standard error are retained in paper_effect (type other); this estimates the local average effect for compliers and is not a standardized effect or a second randomized arm configuration (PDF p. 12, Section 3.3). Both estimands use the full reported analysis sample and belong to the same outcome/arm contrast. The paper's raw similarity signs are retained. Both arms could use ordinary online resources during the learning phase, so the comparison is ai_vs_bau (PDF p. 53, Figure A2). No treatment mean, arm SD, arm-mean SE, exact p-value, test statistic, or numeric confidence limits are printed. No arm mean was reconstructed from an adjusted regression coefficient. The outcome-specific treated count is not separately printed and remains null; it was not obtained by subtraction or borrowed from another analysis. The analysis uses a student-level similarity average rather than treating individual essay pairs as the observations, with participant-level robust SEs; no adjustment for shared-essay dependence or lab/time-slot clustering is reported. Figures 6 and A7 show standardized effects and confidence intervals only graphically (PDF pp. 34 and 58); no values were read from their positions. Repeated assessments do not make the randomized AI-access comparison a within-person crossover. AI availability refers to the assigned AI-allowed arm, regardless of whether a student actually used the tool. Diversity measured while AI is available answers across_people.

Both estimands use the full reported analysis sample and belong to the same outcome/arm contrast. The paper's raw similarity signs are retained. Both arms could use ordinary online resources during the learning phase, so the comparison is ai_vs_bau (PDF p. 53, Figure A2). No treatment mean, arm SD, arm-mean SE, exact p-value, test statistic, or numeric confidence limits are printed. No arm mean was reconstructed from an adjusted regression coefficient. The outcome-specific treated count is not separately printed and remains null; it was not obtained by subtraction or borrowed from another analysis. The analysis uses a student-level similarity average rather than treating individual essay pairs as the observations, with participant-level robust SEs; no adjustment for shared-essay dependence or lab/time-slot clustering is reported. open_items: Neither treatment-arm mean similarity is printed; Table 5 gives control means and adjusted ITT/TOT coefficients. Arm levels remain incomplete because adjusted coefficients cannot be added to unadjusted means (PDF p. 41).

The paper does not print similarity SDs, arm-mean SEs, exact p-values, test statistics, or numeric confidence limits. Figures 6 and A7 show standardized similarity effects and intervals only graphically (PDF pp. 34 and 58).

The outcome-specific treated count is not separately printed for either similarity analysis. n_treatment remains null; the printed control and total counts are retained without subtraction (PDF p. 41, Table 5 Panel B).
The precise MPNet-based embedding checkpoint and the number of essay pairs are not stated (PDF p. 41, Table 5 notes).

Complete outcome-specific missing-essay accounting is not provided. The September Table 5 counts agree with its writing-style Table A4; the earlier screening form's July table-count conflict is superseded. The empty/short-essay rule for AI grading does not establish similarity-analysis exclusions (PDF pp. 41, 66, and 75).

No covariance or cluster adjustment for shared essays in the similarity averages is reported. se_basis describes the paper's participant-level robust uncertainty and does not certify an adjustment for this dependence (PDF pp. 11-12 and 41).
The GPT-4o release year is not printed in the paper; ai_tool.year remains null (PDF p. 8).
